Command Line versus Graphical Interface

Neither interface is universally better. Each has strengths, and skilled users move between them according to the task.

Aspect Command-line interface Graphical user interface

Learning curve Steeper at first; commands must be learned or looked up

Gentler; options are visible in menus and buttons

Speed for repeated tasks Very fast once learned; tasks can be automated

Slower; usually requires repeated clicking

Resource use Very light; ideal for servers and remote work

Heavier; needs display, memory, and graphics support

Precision High; exact options and targets are stated

Varies; depends on what the interface exposes

Automation Natural; commands can be saved as scripts

Limited; often needs special automation tools

Discoverability Lower; requires documentation and practice

Higher; features can be explored visually

Remote administration Excellent over slow connections Possible but bandwidth-hungry

Many professionals combine the two. A developer may edit code in a graphical editor, run tests in a terminal, and view results in a browser. Learning the command line expands what you can do rather than replacing the graphical tools you already know.

The Anatomy of a Command

Most commands follow a consistent structure: a command name, optional options (also called flags or switches), and optional arguments.

Chapter 1: Introduction

1.6 The parts of a typical command line. The first word names the program; options modify its behavior; arguments

identify what it works on.

The command is the name of the program, built-in shell function, or script to run. Options usually begin with a single hyphen followed by a letter, such as -l, or with two hyphens followed by a word, such as --human-readable. Short options can often be combined, so ls -l -h can be written ls -lh. Arguments are the objects the command works on, such as file names, directory names, or text to search for. The shell separates the pieces by spaces, which is why file names containing spaces require special care, as you will see later.

$ ls $ ls -l $ ls -lh /var/log $ ls --all --human-readable

Some options take their own value, such as head -n 5 notes.txt, which asks for the first five lines of notes.txt. Commands are case-sensitive on Linux and macOS: ls works, but LS does not. The same is not true for the Windows Command Prompt, which ignores case for commands.

Exit Status

Every command, when it finishes, returns a small integer called its exit status to the shell. By convention, zero means success and any non-zero value means some kind of failure. You can view the status of the most recent command with the special variable $?.

$ ls /etc $ echo $? 0 $ ls /nonexistent ls: cannot access '/nonexistent': No such file or directory $ echo $? 2

Exit statuses are essential to scripting, because they let a script decide what to do next based on whether a command succeeded.

Chapter 1: Introduction

1.7 How a Command Runs

When you type a command and press Enter, a sequence of steps occurs. The shell first reads and parses the line, splitting it into words and expanding special characters such as wildcards and variables. It then decides what the first word refers to: a built-in command that the shell itself implements, a function or alias, or an external program found on disk. For external programs, the shell searches the directories listed in the PATH environment variable, in order, until it finds an executable file with the requested name.

To run an external program, the shell uses two operating system operations. It creates a copy of itself, known as a child process, using a call named fork. The child then replaces itself with the requested program using a call named exec. Meanwhile, the original shell waits. When the program finishes, the shell receives its exit status and displays a new prompt.

The life cycle of an external command: the shell forks a child, the child executes the program, and the shell waits for completion.

You can ask the shell how it will interpret a name with the type command, and find the file for an external program with which.

$ type cd cd is a shell builtin $ type ls ls is aliased to 'ls --color=auto' $ which grep /usr/bin/grep

Key Idea

Built-in commands, such as cd, run inside the shell itself. External commands, such as grep, are separate programs stored as files and run in child processes. This is why cd must be a built-in: a child process could not change the directory of its parent.

Chapter 2: Real-Life Applications

2.1 Real-Life Applications

The command line appears in everyday professional work more than most people realize.

• Software development: Developers use version control, compilers, test runners, and package managers through commands. A single command can run thousands of automated tests.

• System administration: Administrators create user accounts, adjust permissions, restart services, and read logs on remote servers, often dozens at a time.

• Data analysis: Large text and CSV files can be filtered, counted, and reshaped with a few commands before being loaded into a specialized tool.

• Cloud and DevOps: Infrastructure is described and controlled through command-line tools, and deployment pipelines are scripts of commands.

• Cybersecurity: Analysts examine logs, inspect network connections, and test systems using command-line tools.

• Education and research: Researchers run simulations and process datasets on remote clusters that offer only a shell.

Lesson Summary

A command-line interface lets you control a computer by typing commands. The terminal displays the conversation, the shell interprets it, and utilities carry out the work. A command consists of a name, options, and arguments, and every command returns an exit status. Built-in commands run inside the shell, while external commands are programs located through the PATH variable and started with fork and exec. Understanding these fundamentals prepares you for everything that follows.

Shells and Terminal Environments

Common Shells

Many shells exist, and they share a family resemblance. Knowing the main ones helps you understand documentation, scripts, and the differences between systems.

Shell Description Typical use

Bash The Bourne Again Shell from the GNU Project. Combines Bourne shell scripting with history, command-line editing, and many extensions.

Default on most Linux distributions; widely used for scripts

Zsh A feature-rich shell with advanced completion, spelling correction, and theming. Largely compatible with Bash for everyday use.

Default login shell on recent macOS versions

Fish A user-friendly shell with automatic suggestions and syntax highlighting out of the box. Its scripting syntax differs from Bash.

Interactive use by people who want a friendly experience

Chapter 2: Real-Life Applications

2.2 Shell

Description Typical use

sh (POSIX shell) The standard shell language defined by POSIX. On many systems it is a small, fast shell such as Dash.

Portable scripts that must run anywhere

cmd.exe The traditional Windows Command Prompt, descended from MS-DOS.

Legacy scripts and simple Windows tasks

PowerShell A shell and scripting language from Microsoft that passes .NET objects through pipelines. Available on Windows, macOS, and Linux.

Windows administration and cross-platform automation

You can find out which shell you are using with echo $SHELL, which prints your default login shell, or ps -p $$, which shows the process running your current shell. To try another shell temporarily, simply type its name, such as zsh, and type exit to return.

The Prompt

The prompt is the text the shell prints to show that it is ready for a command. A typical Bash prompt on Linux looks like the following.

student@laptop:~/projects$

This prompt tells you the current user (student), the machine name (laptop), the current directory (~/projects, where the tilde stands for your home directory), and the type of user: a dollar sign indicates an ordinary user, while a hash symbol indicates the administrator account, usually called root. Prompts are customizable; many people add information such as the current Git branch or the time.

Environment Variables

The shell keeps a collection of named values called environment variables. Programs started from the shell inherit copies of them, which lets you configure behavior without changing the programs themselves. Some of the most important ones follow.

Variable Purpose Example value

HOME The current user's home directory /home/student

PATH Colon-separated list of directories searched for commands

/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin

USER The name of the current user student

SHELL The user's default shell /bin/bash

PWD The current working directory /home/student/projects

EDITOR The preferred text editor for programs that need one nano

LANG Language and locale settings en_US.UTF-8

Chapter 2: Real-Life Applications

2.3 Display a variable by placing a dollar sign in front of its name, and set one with an equals sign and no

spaces around it. Use export to make the variable available to programs that the shell starts.

$ echo $HOME /home/student $ GREETING="Hello" $ echo "$GREETING, world" Hello, world $ export EDITOR=nano $ printenv EDITOR nano

The PATH variable deserves special attention. When you type a command name, the shell checks each directory in PATH from left to right. If you install a program in a directory that is not listed, the shell will report that the command was not found. To add a directory to your PATH for the current session, use a line such as export PATH="$PATH:$HOME/bin".

Startup Files

When a shell starts, it can read configuration files that set variables, define aliases, and customize the prompt. For Bash, interactive non-login shells read ~/.bashrc, while login shells read ~/.bash_profile or ~/.profile. Zsh uses ~/.zshrc for interactive shells. Editing these files lets you keep your customizations permanently. After changing one, apply it to the current session with the source command, for example source ~/.bashrc.

Getting Help

No one memorizes every option of every command. Skilled users are distinguished by how well they find answers quickly. Unix-like systems include several built-in help mechanisms.

• man: displays the manual page for a command, such as man ls. Press the space bar to page down, the letter q to quit, and the slash key followed by a word to search.

• --help: most GNU commands print a short usage summary with command --help.

• info: displays longer GNU documentation in a hyperlinked format.

• apropos: searches manual page descriptions by keyword; apropos copy lists commands related to copying. The command man -k does the same.

• type and help: type explains how the shell interprets a name, and help cd shows documentation for Bash built-ins.

• tldr and online resources: community-maintained summaries and official documentation sites provide practical examples.

Manual pages are divided into numbered sections. Section 1 covers user commands, section 5 covers file formats, and section 8 covers system administration commands. When a name exists in several sections, you can specify one, as in man 5 passwd to read about the password file format rather than the passwd command.

Chapter 2: Real-Life Applications

2.4 Reading a Manual Page

A manual page typically contains these parts: NAME, a one-line description; SYNOPSIS, showing how the command is used; DESCRIPTION, explaining behavior and options; EXAMPLES, in some pages; and SEE ALSO, which lists related topics. In a synopsis, square brackets mark optional items, and an ellipsis indicates that an item can repeat. Learning to read a synopsis is one of the most valuable command-line skills.

Keyboard Shortcuts and Editing

Modern shells offer powerful line editing. These shortcuts work in Bash and many other shells and can dramatically speed up your work.

Shortcut Effect

Tab Completes a command, file name, or directory name; press twice to list possibilities

Up and Down arrows Browse previous commands from history

Ctrl+C Interrupts (stops) the running command

Ctrl+D Signals end of input; at an empty prompt it logs out or exits the shell

Ctrl+L Clears the screen

Ctrl+A and Ctrl+E Moves the cursor to the start or end of the line

Ctrl+R Searches backward through command history

Ctrl+U and Ctrl+K Deletes from the cursor to the start or end of the line

Ctrl+Z Suspends the running command (it can be resumed later)

Tab completion alone saves a great deal of typing and prevents typing mistakes. Get into the habit of pressing Tab frequently.

Command History

The shell records the commands you type. The history command lists them with numbers, and you can repeat an earlier one with an exclamation mark and its number, such as !42. The expression !! repeats the previous command, which is handy in the form sudo !! when you forgot to use administrator privileges. Press Ctrl+R and begin typing to search your history interactively. Be aware that history can capture sensitive information typed on the command line, such as passwords passed as arguments, so avoid typing secrets directly into commands.

Lesson Summary

Shells differ in features and syntax, but they share concepts: a prompt, environment variables, startup files, history, and completion. The PATH variable determines where commands are found, and the manual system provides authoritative help. Mastering the keyboard shortcuts and help tools makes every later lesson easier.

Chapter 2: Real-Life Applications

2.5 Navigating the Filesystem

The Filesystem Hierarchy

Unix-like systems organize all files in a single tree that begins at the root directory, written as a single slash. Unlike Windows, which assigns drive letters such as C: and D:, Linux and macOS attach additional storage devices to directories within the same tree, a process called mounting. The Filesystem Hierarchy Standard describes the conventional layout used by Linux distributions.

A simplified view of the Linux directory tree. Every file lives somewhere below the root directory.

Directory Typical contents

/ The root of the entire tree

/bin and /usr/bin Essential user commands and programs, such as ls and cp

/sbin and /usr/sbin System administration commands

/etc System-wide configuration files, mostly plain text

/home Home directories of ordinary users

/root Home directory of the administrator account

/var Variable data that changes while the system runs, such as logs, caches, and mail

/tmp Temporary files, often cleared at reboot

/usr Programs, libraries, and documentation installed with the system

/dev Special files that represent devices, such as disks and terminals

/proc and /sys Virtual files that expose information about processes and the kernel

/mnt and /media Mount points for additional file systems and removable media

On macOS, user home directories are in /Users, and the layout includes additional directories specific to that system. The concepts, however, are the same.

Chapter 2: Real-Life Applications

2.6 Paths: Absolute and Relative

A path is a string that identifies a file or directory by describing where it sits in the tree. An absolute path starts at the root and therefore begins with a slash, such as /home/student/projects/notes.txt. It means the same thing no matter where you currently are. A relative path starts from the current working directory and does not begin with a slash, such as projects/notes.txt.

Two special names are available in every directory. A single dot refers to the current directory, and two dots refer to its parent directory. The tilde character is shorthand for your home directory. A path such as ../shared/data.csv means: go up one level, enter a directory named shared, and select data.csv.

Moving Around

Three commands handle most navigation.

$ pwd /home/student $ cd projects $ pwd /home/student/projects $ cd .. $ cd /var/log $ cd ~ $ cd -

The command pwd prints the working directory. The command cd changes it; used alone or with a tilde it returns to your home directory, and cd - returns to the previous directory. The command ls lists the contents of a directory.

Listing Files with ls

The ls command has many useful options.

Option Effect

-l Long format: permissions, owner, group, size, modification time, and name

-a Show all files, including hidden ones whose names begin with a dot

-h With -l, show sizes in human-readable units such as K, M, and G

-t Sort by modification time, newest first

-r Reverse the sort order

-S Sort by file size, largest first

-R List subdirectories recursively

-d List directories themselves rather than their contents

A long listing looks like this.

Chapter 2: Real-Life Applications

2.7 $ ls -lh

total 12K drwxr-xr-x 2 student student 4.0K Mar 3 09:14 docs -rw-r--r-- 1 student student 1.2K Mar 3 09:20 notes.txt -rwxr-xr-x 1 student student 215 Mar 4 11:02 backup.sh

Each line describes one item. The first character shows the type: a hyphen for a regular file, d for a directory, and l for a symbolic link. The next nine characters show permissions, which you will study in a later chapter. The following fields give the number of links, the owner, the group, the size, the modification date, and the name.

Hidden Files

On Unix-like systems, files whose names begin with a dot are hidden from ordinary listings. They are typically configuration files, such as .bashrc or .gitconfig. Use ls -a to see them. Hiding is a convenience for reducing clutter, not a security feature.

Viewing the Structure with tree and find

The tree command, available through package managers on many systems, draws a directory hierarchy. For a quick look at a limited depth, use tree -L 2. When tree is not installed, find can list contents, and ls -R provides a recursive listing. The find command is covered in detail in the next chapter.

File Names and Special Characters

Linux file names may contain almost any character except the slash and the null character, but some choices cause trouble. Spaces separate arguments, so a file named My Notes.txt must be quoted or escaped: cat "My Notes.txt" or cat My\ Notes.txt. A file name that begins with a hyphen can be mistaken for an option; the notation -- marks the end of options, as in rm -- -strange-file. For maximum portability, many professionals prefer names with lowercase letters, digits, hyphens, and underscores.

Common Mistake

Linux file names are case-sensitive. Report.txt, report.txt, and REPORT.TXT are three different files. On Windows and, by default, macOS, they would refer to the same file.

Links: Hard and Symbolic

A link lets one file be reached by more than one name. A hard link is another directory entry that points to the same underlying data; the data remains until every hard link is removed. Hard links cannot cross file systems and normally cannot point to directories. A symbolic link, or symlink, is a special small file that contains a path to another file, similar to a shortcut. Symlinks can cross file systems and point to directories, but they break if the target is moved or deleted.

$ ln original.txt hardlink.txt $ ln -s original.txt softlink.txt

Chapter 3: $ ls -l

3.1 $ ls -l

-rw-r--r-- 2 student student 120 Mar 5 10:00 hardlink.txt -rw-r--r-- 2 student student 120 Mar 5 10:00 original.txt lrwxrwxrwx 1 student student 12 Mar 5 10:01 softlink.txt -> original.txt

Lesson Summary

The filesystem is a single tree rooted at a slash. Paths locate items absolutely or relative to the working directory. The commands pwd, cd, and ls are the foundation of navigation, and options such as -l, -a, and -h reveal details. Hidden files, case sensitivity, spaces in names, and links are practical details that you will meet regularly.

Working with Files and Directories

Creating Files and Directories

The mkdir command creates directories, and touch creates an empty file or updates the modification time of an existing one.

$ mkdir practice $ mkdir -p practice/reports/2025 $ touch practice/notes.txt $ ls -R practice

The -p option of mkdir creates any missing parent directories and does not complain if the directory already exists. To create a file with content, you can use a text editor such as nano, which shows its key commands at the bottom of the screen, or vim, a powerful editor that takes longer to learn. You can also create content with redirection, as described in a later chapter.

Copying, Moving, and Renaming

The cp command copies files, mv moves or renames them, and rm removes them.

$ cp notes.txt notes-backup.txt $ cp -r reports reports-copy $ mv notes.txt archive/ $ mv draft.txt final.txt $ rm old.txt $ rm -r old-folder

The -r (recursive) option is required to copy or remove directories and everything inside them. The mv command has no separate rename command: renaming is simply moving to a new name. Useful safety options include -i, which asks for confirmation before overwriting or deleting, and -v, which prints what is being done.

Chapter 3: $ ls -l

3.2 Caution

The rm command does not use a recycle bin. Deleted files are generally gone. Never run commands such as rm -rf with a path you have not double-checked, and be especially careful with wildcards. The command rm -rf / is catastrophic in older systems, and modern versions of rm refuse it by default, but mistakes with similar commands can still destroy important data.

Wildcards and Globbing

The shell can expand special characters, called wildcards or glob patterns, into matching file names before the command runs. This is a powerful shortcut for working with many files at once.

Pattern Meaning Example

* Matches any number of characters, including none

ls *.txt lists all files ending in .txt

? Matches exactly one character ls file?.txt matches file1.txt and fileA.txt

[abc] Matches one character from the set ls report[123].txt

[a-z] Matches one character in the range ls [a-c]*.log

{a,b} Brace expansion: generates each alternative (done by the shell, not a file match)

mkdir project/{src,docs,tests}

Because the shell performs expansion, the program never sees the pattern. If you type ls *.txt and three files match, the program receives three file names. Quoting a pattern, as in "*.txt", prevents expansion.

Quoting

Quotes control how the shell interprets special characters. Single quotes preserve every character literally. Double quotes preserve most characters literally but still allow variable expansion and command substitution. A backslash escapes the next single character.

$ NAME="Ada" $ echo 'Hello, $NAME' Hello, $NAME $ echo "Hello, $NAME" Hello, Ada $ echo "Today is $(date +%A)"

The expression $(command) is called command substitution: it runs the command and substitutes its output into the line. As a rule, always put double quotes around variable expansions in scripts, such as "$file", to avoid problems with spaces.

Viewing File Contents

Several utilities display files in different ways.

Chapter 3: $ ls -l

3.3 Command

Purpose

cat file Prints the entire file; can also join several files together

less file Shows a file one screen at a time, with scrolling and searching; press q to quit

head -n 10 file Shows the first 10 lines

tail -n 10 file Shows the last 10 lines

tail -f file Follows a file as new lines are added, useful for watching logs

wc file Counts lines, words, and bytes

file name Identifies the type of a file by examining its content

stat file Displays detailed information such as size, permissions, and timestamps

Use less rather than cat for long files, since cat floods the screen. Inside less, press the slash key to search forward, n to repeat the search, and g or G to jump to the beginning or end.

Finding Files with find and locate

The find command searches a directory tree for files that match conditions. Its general form is the starting directory followed by tests and actions.

$ find . -name "*.txt" $ find /var/log -type f -size +1M $ find . -type d -name "backup*" $ find . -mtime -7 $ find . -name "*.tmp" -delete $ find . -name "*.sh" -exec chmod +x {} \;

Common tests are -name for the file name pattern (use -iname to ignore case), -type where f means file and d means directory, -size for size, -mtime for modification time in days, and -user for owner. The -exec action runs a command for each match, with the braces replaced by the file name. The locate command searches a prebuilt index and is much faster, but its index may be out of date; update it with sudo updatedb.

Disk Usage

Two utilities report on storage. The df command shows free and used space on mounted file systems, and du shows how much space files and directories use.

$ df -h $ du -sh ~/Documents $ du -h --max-depth=1 /var | sort -h

The -h option gives human-readable sizes. The expression du -sh prints a single summarized total for each argument. The command du -h --max-depth=1 /var | sort -h is a good example of combining utilities to find which subdirectory uses the most space. Note that --max-depth is a GNU option; on macOS the equivalent is -d 1.

Chapter 3: $ ls -l

3.4 Archives and Compression

An archive bundles many files into one file, and compression reduces its size. On Unix-like systems the tar command creates and extracts archives, and it is commonly combined with compression by gzip, producing files that end in .tar.gz or .tgz.

$ tar -czvf backup.tar.gz documents/ $ tar -tzvf backup.tar.gz $ tar -xzvf backup.tar.gz $ tar -xzvf backup.tar.gz -C /tmp/restore $ gzip bigfile.log $ gunzip bigfile.log.gz $ zip -r project.zip project/ $ unzip project.zip

In tar, the letters have meaning: c creates, x extracts, t lists contents, z uses gzip compression, v is verbose, and f names the archive file, which must come right after the options. Always list an archive with -t before extracting an unfamiliar one so you know where its files will land.

Comparing and Checksums

The diff command shows the differences between two text files, and cmp compares files byte by byte. To confirm that a file was not corrupted or altered, compute a checksum: sha256sum file prints a fingerprint of the content, and comparing it with a published value verifies integrity. On macOS the equivalent is shasum -a 256 file.

Lesson Summary

You can now create, copy, move, delete, view, search, measure, and archive files from the command line. Wildcards and quoting control how the shell prepares your command, and find combined with other commands makes bulk operations possible. Because deletion is permanent, develop careful habits from the beginning.

Chapter 3: $ ls -l

3.5 Text Processing Utilities

Why Text Processing Matters

On Unix-like systems, a great deal of information is stored as plain text: configuration files, logs, source code, data tables, and reports. A family of small utilities exists to search, extract, sort, and transform text. Learned together, they become a flexible toolkit for analyzing information without writing a full program.

Searching with grep

The grep command prints the lines of its input that match a pattern. Its name comes from an editing command for globally searching a regular expression and printing the result.

$ grep "error" server.log $ grep -i "error" server.log $ grep -n "timeout" server.log $ grep -c "404" access.log $ grep -v "debug" server.log $ grep -r "TODO" ~/projects $ grep -E "error|warning" server.log $ grep -w "cat" words.txt

Option Effect

-i Ignore case

-n Show line numbers

-c Print only a count of matching lines

-v Invert: show lines that do not match

-r Search directories recursively

-l List only the names of files that contain a match

-E Use extended regular expressions

-w Match whole words only

-A, -B, -C Show lines after, before, or around each match

Regular Expressions

A regular expression (often shortened to regex) is a compact notation for describing patterns in text. Regular expressions are used by grep, sed, awk, many programming languages, and text editors. Two flavors matter for the command line: basic regular expressions, the default in grep and sed, and extended regular expressions, enabled with grep -E or sed -E, which allow more operators without backslashes.

Chapter 3: $ ls -l

3.6 Element

Meaning Example

. Any single character c.t matches cat and cut

* Zero or more of the previous item ab*c matches ac and abbbc

+ One or more of the previous item (extended) ab+c matches abc but not ac

? Zero or one of the previous item (extended) colou?r matches color and colour

^ Start of a line ^Error matches lines beginning with Error

$ End of a line done$ matches lines ending with done

[abc] Any one character in the set [0-9] matches a digit

[^abc] Any one character not in the set [^0-9] matches a non-digit

a|b Alternation: either side (extended) (jpg|png) matches either word

\ Escapes a special character \. matches a literal dot

$ grep -E "^[A-Z][a-z]+ [0-9]{4}$" list.txt $ grep -E "[0-9]{3}-[0-9]{4}" contacts.txt $ grep -E "^$" file.txt

The first example matches lines made of a capitalized word, a space, and a four-digit number. The last matches empty lines. Build regular expressions step by step and test each piece on sample data.

Sorting and Removing Duplicates

The sort command orders lines, and uniq collapses adjacent duplicate lines, so input is usually sorted first.

$ sort names.txt $ sort -r names.txt $ sort -n numbers.txt $ sort -t, -k2 data.csv $ sort names.txt | uniq $ sort names.txt | uniq -c $ sort names.txt | uniq -d

Options include -n for numeric order (without it, 10 sorts before 2), -r to reverse, -u to remove duplicates, -k to sort by a specific field, and -t to set the field separator. With uniq, -c prefixes each line with the number of occurrences and -d shows only duplicated lines.

Cutting, Joining, and Translating

The cut command extracts columns. For delimited text, give a delimiter with -d and the field numbers with -f.

$ cut -d, -f1,3 data.csv $ cut -d: -f1 /etc/passwd

Chapter 3: $ ls -l

3.7 $ cut -c1-10 file.txt

The paste command merges lines of files side by side, and join combines files on a common field. The tr command translates or deletes individual characters from standard input.

$ echo "Hello World" | tr 'a-z' 'A-Z' HELLO WORLD $ echo "a b c" | tr -s ' ' a b c $ tr -d '\r' < windows.txt > unix.txt

The wc command counts: wc -l counts lines, wc -w counts words, and wc -c counts bytes. The tee command copies its input both to the screen and to a file, which is useful for saving the output of a pipeline while still watching it.

Stream Editing with sed

The sed command is a stream editor: it reads text, applies editing commands, and writes the result. Its most famous use is substitution.

$ sed 's/cat/dog/' pets.txt $ sed 's/cat/dog/g' pets.txt $ sed -n '5,10p' file.txt $ sed '/^#/d' config.conf $ sed -i 's/http:/https:/' links.txt $ sed -i.bak 's/foo/bar/' file.txt

In s/old/new/, the first match on each line is replaced; adding the g flag replaces all matches on the line. The -n option suppresses automatic printing, and the p command prints selected lines. The d command deletes lines. The -i option edits the file in place, which modifies your original, so it is wise to supply a backup suffix as in -i.bak until you are confident. Note that on macOS, the in-place option requires an argument for the suffix, so sed -i '' ... is used for no backup.

Pattern Scanning with awk

The awk utility is a small programming language for processing text organized in records and fields. By default, each line is a record and whitespace separates fields, which are referred to as $1, $2, and so on, with $0 meaning the whole line. An awk program consists of pattern and action pairs.

$ awk '{print $1}' access.log $ awk -F: '{print $1, $3}' /etc/passwd $ awk '$3 > 100 {print $1}' data.txt $ awk '{sum += $2} END {print sum}' sales.txt $ awk 'NR > 1 {print $2}' data.txt

The -F option sets the field separator. The condition $3 > 100 selects only lines where the third field is greater than 100. The special pattern END runs after all input is processed, which is ideal for totals. The variable NR holds the current record number, and NF holds the number of fields on the line.

Chapter 4: A Worked Example: Analyzing a Web Server Log

4.1 A Worked Example: Analyzing a Web Server Log

Imagine a log file where each line begins with the visitor's address, followed by other fields including the status code. To find the five addresses that appear most often, chain utilities.

$ awk '{print $1}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -5

Reading left to right: awk extracts the first field of every line, sort groups identical addresses, uniq -c counts each group, sort -rn orders by count from highest to lowest, and head -5 keeps the top five. Each program does one simple job, and together they answer a real question in a single line.

Running Commands on Lists with xargs

Some commands read file names from their arguments rather than from standard input. The xargs command converts input lines into arguments for another command.

$ find . -name "*.log" | xargs wc -l $ find . -name "*.tmp" -print0 | xargs -0 rm

When file names may contain spaces, use the null-separated form: -print0 with find and -0 with xargs.

Comparing Files with diff

$ diff old.txt new.txt $ diff -u old.txt new.txt

The unified format produced by -u shows removed lines prefixed with a minus sign and added lines prefixed with a plus sign. It is the format used by patches and version control systems.

Lesson Summary

Text processing utilities turn the command line into an analytical tool. grep finds lines, regular expressions describe patterns, sort and uniq organize and count, cut and tr reshape fields and characters, sed edits streams, and awk handles field-based calculations. Their real strength appears when you combine them in pipelines, the subject of the next chapter.

Chapter 4: A Worked Example: Analyzing a Web Server Log

4.2 Input, Output, and Pipelines

Standard Streams

Every command line program starts with three communication channels, called standard streams. Standard input (stdin, file descriptor 0) is where the program reads data, which by default is the keyboard. Standard output (stdout, descriptor 1) is where the program writes normal results, which by default is the terminal screen. Standard error (stderr, descriptor 2) is a separate channel for error messages, also displayed on the screen by default. Keeping errors apart from results means you can save or process one without the other.

The three standard streams of a process. Each can be redirected independently to or from files.

Redirection

Redirection changes where a stream is connected. The shell sets this up before the program runs, so the program itself does not need to know.

Operator Meaning Example

> Send standard output to a file, replacing its contents ls > list.txt

>> Append standard output to the end of a file date >> log.txt

< Read standard input from a file sort < names.txt

2> Send standard error to a file find / -name x 2> errors.txt

2>> Append standard error to a file make 2>> build-errors.txt

&> or > file 2>&1

Send both output and errors to the same file make &> build.log

2>/dev/null Discard error messages find / -name x 2>/dev/null

$ echo "First line" > notes.txt $ echo "Second line" >> notes.txt

Chapter 4: A Worked Example: Analyzing a Web Server Log

4.3 $ cat notes.txt

First line Second line $ wc -l < notes.txt 2 $ ls /nonexistent 2> errors.txt $ ls /etc /nonexistent > out.txt 2> err.txt

The special file /dev/null accepts any data and discards it, which makes it a convenient way to silence unwanted output. The form 2>&1 means send descriptor 2 to wherever descriptor 1 is currently going, so command > all.txt 2>&1 captures both streams in one file. The order matters: the redirection of standard output must come first.

Caution

A single greater-than sign overwrites the target file immediately, even before the command finishes. Typing sort data.txt > data.txt empties data.txt before sort reads it. Redirect to a different file, then rename it.

Here Documents and Here Strings

A here document supplies multiple lines of input directly inside a script or on the command line, ending at a chosen marker word. A here string supplies a single string.

$ cat << EOF > greeting.txt Hello, This text goes into the file. EOF $ grep "apple" <<< "apple pie"

Pipelines

A pipeline connects the standard output of one command directly to the standard input of the next using the vertical bar character. Data flows through memory, and the commands run at the same time, so the second can begin work before the first has finished.

A pipeline: each command performs one small step and passes its output to the next.

$ cat access.log | grep " 404 " | sort | uniq -c $ ls -l | wc -l

Chapter 4: A Worked Example: Analyzing a Web Server Log

4.4 $ history | grep ssh

$ ps aux | grep nginx $ du -h /var | sort -rh | head -10

Pipelines embody a central idea of the Unix philosophy: build complex behavior by combining simple tools. When you design a pipeline, add one stage at a time and check the output at each stage. If a pipeline produces surprising results, run it again with later stages removed to see where the data changed.

By default, only standard output flows through a pipe. To include error messages, redirect first, as in command 2>&1 | grep problem. The exit status of a pipeline is normally that of its last command; in Bash, the option set -o pipefail makes a pipeline report failure if any stage fails.

Command Lists and Conditional Execution

You can place several commands on one line.

Operator Meaning Example

; Run the next command regardless of the first one's result

cd docs; ls

&& Run the next command only if the first succeeded mkdir backup && cp *.txt backup

|| Run the next command only if the first failed cd data || echo "No such folder"

& Run the command in the background sleep 60 &

The combination of && and || gives simple if-then logic on a single line: test -f config.txt && echo "found" || echo "missing". Be cautious, however, because the command after || also runs if the one after && fails.

Substitution and Subshells

Command substitution, $(command), was introduced earlier. Related features include process substitution, which in Bash lets you compare the output of two commands as if they were files, as in diff <(sort a.txt) <(sort b.txt). Grouping commands in parentheses runs them in a subshell, a separate child shell whose changes to variables and directories do not affect the parent.

Lesson Summary

Streams, redirection, and pipelines form the heart of command-line power. Standard input, output, and error can be redirected to files or discarded. Pipelines combine small programs into precise tools, and operators such as && and || let a line react to success or failure.

Chapter 4: A Worked Example: Analyzing a Web Server Log

4.5 Users, Permissions, and Ownership

Why Permissions Exist

Unix-like systems are multi-user systems. Even a laptop used by one person runs many programs under different accounts so that a mistake or a malicious program cannot easily damage everything. Every file has an owner, a group, and a set of permissions that determine who may read, change, or run it. These controls protect private data, prevent accidental deletion of system files, and limit the damage a compromised program can do.

Users and Groups

Each account has a numeric user identifier (UID) and belongs to one or more groups, each with a group identifier (GID). The account with UID 0, called root, is the administrator and may do almost anything. Information about accounts is stored in files such as /etc/passwd, and group definitions are in /etc/group. The following commands show identity information.

$ whoami student $ id uid=1000(student) gid=1000(student) groups=1000(student),27(sudo) $ groups student sudo

Reading Permission Strings

The long listing from ls -l displays a ten-character permission string. The first character is the file type. The remaining nine are three groups of three, for the owner (user), the group, and others (everyone else). In each group, r means read, w means write, and x means execute, while a hyphen means the permission is absent.

Reading a permission string and converting it to octal notation.

Chapter 4: A Worked Example: Analyzing a Web Server Log

4.6 The meaning of each permission depends on whether the item is a file or a directory.

Permission On a regular file On a directory

Read (r) View the contents List the names of the contents

Write (w) Modify the contents Create, rename, or delete entries inside

Execute (x) Run the file as a program Enter the directory and access items within it

Changing Permissions with chmod

The chmod command changes permissions. It supports two notations. In symbolic mode you state who (u for user, g for group, o for others, a for all), an operator (plus, minus, or equals), and the permissions.

$ chmod u+x script.sh $ chmod g-w shared.txt $ chmod a+r public.html $ chmod u=rwx,g=rx,o=r program

In octal mode each group of permissions is written as a digit that sums read as 4, write as 2, and execute as 1. Three digits describe owner, group, and others.

Octal Permissions Typical use

rw------- Private file such as an SSH private key

rw-r--r-- Ordinary document readable by everyone

rwx------ Private script or directory

rwxr-xr-x Program or public directory

rwxrwxr-x Directory shared with a group

r-------- Read-only secret

$ chmod 755 backup.sh $ chmod 600 ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 $ chmod -R 755 website/

Changing Ownership

The chown command changes the owner and group of a file, and chgrp changes only the group. Changing ownership generally requires administrator privileges.

$ sudo chown alice report.txt $ sudo chown alice:developers project/ $ sudo chown -R www-data:www-data /var/www/site

Chapter 4: A Worked Example: Analyzing a Web Server Log

4.7 Default Permissions and umask

When a new file is created, the system starts from a default and removes the bits in the umask. With the common umask of 022, new files are created as 644 and new directories as 755. Run umask to see the current value. A stricter value such as 077 gives new items to the owner only.

Administrator Access: su and sudo

Daily work should be done as an ordinary user, and administrative power used only when required. The sudo command runs one command with the privileges of another user, normally root, after checking that the current user is authorized and, typically, asking for the user's own password.

$ sudo apt update $ sudo systemctl restart nginx $ sudo -l

The command su starts a shell as another user, and sudo -i opens a root shell. The principle of least privilege says that a user or program should have only the access needed to do its job. Avoid logging in as root and avoid running programs with sudo unless necessary, since an error made with root authority can do far more harm.

Special Permission Bits

Three special bits exist. The setuid bit makes a program run with the privileges of its owner rather than the user who launched it; the passwd command uses this so that ordinary users can change their own passwords. The setgid bit on a directory causes new files inside to inherit the directory's group, which helps shared folders. The sticky bit on a directory, as on /tmp, allows only a file's owner to delete or rename it. Special bits are shown as s or t in the permission string and set with a leading fourth octal digit, such as chmod 1777 /shared.

Lesson Summary

Permissions determine who may read, write, and execute each file. They are displayed in listings, changed with chmod, and tied to ownership managed by chown. The umask sets defaults, and sudo provides controlled administrative access. Applying the principle of least privilege keeps systems safer.

Chapter 5: Processes and System Monitoring

5.1 Processes and System Monitoring

What Is a Process?

A process is a running instance of a program. Each process has a process identifier (PID), a parent process, an owner, memory, and open files. When you run a command, you create a process; the shell itself is a process. The operating system's scheduler divides processor time among all processes, switching so rapidly that they appear to run simultaneously.

Common states in the life of a process.

Viewing Processes

The ps command takes a snapshot of processes. The most common forms are ps aux, which lists every process with its owner, CPU use, and memory use, and ps -ef, which gives a full-format listing including parent process identifiers.

$ ps aux | head -3 $ ps -ef | grep ssh $ pgrep -l firefox $ pstree -p

For a live, continuously updating view, use top, or the friendlier htop if it is installed. In top, the header summarizes load, tasks, CPU, and memory, and the table lists processes sorted by activity. Press q to quit.

Column Meaning

PID The process identifier

USER The account that owns the process

%CPU Share of processor time being used

%MEM Share of physical memory being used

Chapter 5: Processes and System Monitoring

5.2 Column

Meaning

STAT State code: R running, S sleeping, T stopped, Z zombie

COMMAND The program that started the process

The load average shown by uptime gives the average number of processes waiting to run over the last one, five, and fifteen minutes. As a rough guide, a load consistently higher than the number of processor cores suggests the system is overloaded.

Foreground and Background Jobs

A command normally runs in the foreground and holds the prompt until it finishes. You can start a command in the background by adding an ampersand, or suspend a foreground command with Ctrl+Z and continue it in the background.

$ sleep 300 & [1] 4521 $ jobs [1]+ Running sleep 300 & $ fg %1 $ bg %1

The jobs command lists the shell's jobs, fg brings one to the foreground, and bg resumes a suspended one in the background. Background jobs may be terminated when you close the terminal. To keep a command running after you log out, use nohup command &, or use a terminal multiplexer such as tmux, which is discussed later.

Signals and Ending Processes

A signal is a short message sent to a process. The kill command sends signals despite its name. By default it sends SIGTERM (signal 15), which politely asks the process to terminate and allows it to clean up. If a process ignores that request, SIGKILL (signal 9) forces immediate termination without cleanup.

$ kill 4521 $ kill -9 4521 $ killall firefox $ pkill -f "python script.py"

Signal Number Meaning

SIGHUP 1 Hangup; often used to ask a service to reload its configuration

SIGINT 2 Interrupt; sent by Ctrl+C

SIGKILL 9 Immediate termination that cannot be caught or ignored

SIGTERM 15 Polite request to terminate (the default for kill)

SIGSTOP 19 on Linux Pause a process; cannot be ignored

Chapter 5: Processes and System Monitoring

5.3 Signal

Number Meaning

SIGTSTP 20 on Linux Terminal stop; sent by Ctrl+Z

Try SIGTERM first and use SIGKILL only as a last resort. A process that exits but whose parent has not collected its status is a zombie; it uses almost no resources and disappears when the parent reads its status or itself exits.

Process Priority

The nice command starts a program with a modified priority, and renice changes it for a running process. Niceness values range from -20 (highest priority) to 19 (lowest). Ordinary users may only lower priority, which is a courteous way to run long calculations without slowing other work: nice -n 10 ./long-job.sh.

Memory, Disk, and System Information

Command What it shows

free -h Total, used, and available memory and swap, in human-readable units

df -h Free and used space on each mounted file system

du -sh dir Total space used by a directory

lsblk Block devices such as disks and partitions

uptime How long the system has run, logged-in users, and load average

uname -a Kernel name, version, and machine architecture

lscpu Processor architecture and core information

lsof Open files and the processes using them

vmstat Virtual memory, processes, and processor activity statistics

dmesg Kernel messages, useful for hardware troubleshooting

Services and Logs with systemd

Most modern Linux distributions use systemd to start and manage background programs called services or daemons. The systemctl command controls them.

$ systemctl status ssh $ sudo systemctl start nginx $ sudo systemctl stop nginx $ sudo systemctl restart nginx $ sudo systemctl enable nginx $ systemctl list-units --type=service

The verbs start and stop act immediately, while enable and disable control whether the service starts automatically at boot. Systemd collects log messages in a journal that you read with journalctl.

Chapter 5: Processes and System Monitoring

5.4 $ journalctl -u nginx

$ journalctl -u nginx --since "1 hour ago" $ journalctl -p err -b $ journalctl -f

The -u option filters by service, -p filters by priority, -b limits output to the current boot, and -f follows new messages. Traditional text logs are also found under /var/log, where files such as syslog or auth.log can be examined with tail, grep, and less.

A Troubleshooting Workflow

When a system feels slow, work from broad to specific. Check uptime for the load average, then top or htop to see which process uses the processor or memory. Use free -h to see whether memory is exhausted, df -h to confirm that disks are not full, and journalctl or log files to look for errors. Record what you find before changing anything, so that you can undo your steps.

Lesson Summary

Processes are running programs that you can list, observe, and control. The commands ps, top, jobs, kill, and nice manage them, while free, df, and uptime report on resources. On systemd-based systems, systemctl manages services and journalctl reads their logs. A calm, step-by-step investigation is the habit of an effective administrator.

Networking Utilities

Networking Concepts for the Command Line

Computers communicate over networks using agreed rules called protocols. Each device on an IP network has an IP address, and services are reached through numbered ports; for example, web servers conventionally use port 80 for HTTP and 443 for HTTPS, and SSH uses port 22. Names such as www.example.com are translated to addresses by the Domain Name System (DNS). Command-line tools let you inspect each of these layers, which makes them invaluable for troubleshooting.

Chapter 5: Processes and System Monitoring

5.5 Network layers, representative protocols, and the command-line tools used to examine them.

Inspecting Your Network Configuration

On modern Linux systems the ip command displays and configures network interfaces, addresses, and routes. It replaces the older ifconfig and route commands.

$ ip addr show $ ip link show $ ip route show $ hostname $ hostname -I

The first command lists interface addresses, the second lists interfaces and their state, and the third shows the routing table, including the default gateway. On macOS, ifconfig and networksetup are used, and on Windows ipconfig serves the same purpose.

Testing Connectivity

The ping command sends small ICMP echo requests to a host and reports whether replies arrive and how long they take. On Linux it runs until interrupted unless you limit the count.

$ ping -c 4 example.com $ traceroute example.com $ mtr example.com

Ping answers the first troubleshooting question: can I reach that host at all? The traceroute command shows the sequence of routers a packet passes through, which helps locate where a connection fails. Note that some networks block ICMP, so a failed ping does not always prove a host is down.

Name Resolution with dig and nslookup

The dig utility queries DNS servers and shows detailed answers. The older nslookup is also widely available, including on Windows.

Chapter 5: Processes and System Monitoring

5.6 $ dig example.com

$ dig example.com MX $ dig +short example.com $ nslookup example.com

If a site cannot be reached by name but can be reached by IP address, DNS is the likely culprit.

Connections and Ports

The ss command, which replaces the older netstat, lists sockets and connections.

$ ss -tuln $ ss -tp $ nc -zv example.com 443

In ss -tuln, t selects TCP, u selects UDP, l shows listening sockets, and n displays numeric addresses and ports. The nc (netcat) utility can test whether a port accepts connections, as in the third example.

Transferring Data with curl and wget

The curl command transfers data to or from servers using many protocols, and wget downloads files, including recursively.

$ curl https://example.com $ curl -I https://example.com $ curl -o page.html https://example.com $ curl -L https://example.com/short $ curl -X POST -d "name=Ada" https://example.com/api $ wget https://example.com/file.zip $ wget -c https://example.com/bigfile.iso

With curl, -I fetches only the response headers, -o saves to a named file, and -L follows redirects. The -c option of wget continues an interrupted download. These tools are used constantly for testing web services and automating downloads. Before running a script that you downloaded from the internet, read it first; never pipe unknown downloads directly into a shell.

Remote Access with SSH

Secure Shell (SSH) provides an encrypted connection to a remote machine, giving you a command line there as if you were seated at it. It is the standard way to administer servers.

$ ssh student@server.example.com $ ssh -p 2222 student@server.example.com $ ssh student@server.example.com "uptime" $ ssh-keygen -t ed25519 $ ssh-copy-id student@server.example.com

Chapter 5: Processes and System Monitoring

5.7 SSH supports password login, but key-based authentication is stronger. You generate a pair of

keys: the private key stays secret on your computer, and the public key is placed on the server. The ssh-keygen command creates the pair, and ssh-copy-id installs the public key. Protect the private key, which should have permissions of 600, and never share it. The file ~/.ssh/config can define short names and options for the servers you use often.

Copying Files: scp, sftp, and rsync

$ scp report.pdf student@server:/home/student/ $ scp -r project/ student@server:/home/student/ $ rsync -avz project/ student@server:/backups/project/ $ rsync -av --delete source/ destination/ $ rsync -avn source/ destination/

The scp command copies files over SSH. The rsync utility is more efficient for repeated transfers because it copies only the differences, and it can preserve permissions and timestamps. In rsync -avz, a means archive mode, v means verbose, and z compresses data in transit. A trailing slash on the source directory changes the result: project/ copies the contents, while project copies the directory itself. The -n option performs a dry run showing what would happen, and you should use it before any command involving --delete.

Network Security Basics

Open ports are doors into a system, so expose only those that are needed. Keep software updated, use key-based SSH authentication, disable direct root login over SSH, and use a firewall. On Ubuntu, ufw provides a simple interface, as in sudo ufw allow 22/tcp and sudo ufw enable. Never run commands from untrusted sources without understanding them, and avoid sending passwords through unencrypted protocols such as plain FTP or Telnet.

Lesson Summary

Command-line networking tools reveal the state of each network layer. ip shows configuration, ping and traceroute test reachability, dig checks DNS, ss lists connections, curl and wget transfer data, and ssh, scp, and rsync provide secure remote access and file synchronization.

Chapter 6: Package Management and Software

6.1 Package Management and Software

Installation

What Is a Package Manager?

A package is an archive that contains a program, its files, and metadata describing its version and dependencies, which are other packages it needs. A package manager is a utility that downloads packages from trusted repositories, installs them in the correct places, resolves dependencies, and updates or removes them cleanly. Using a package manager is safer and easier than downloading programs by hand because packages are usually digitally signed and tracked by the system.

A package manager retrieves packages and metadata from repositories and installs them on the system.

Common Package Managers

System Tool Typical commands

Debian, Ubuntu apt sudo apt update; sudo apt install package; sudo apt remove package

Fedora, Red Hat family

dnf sudo dnf install package; sudo dnf upgrade

Arch Linux pacman sudo pacman -S package; sudo pacman -Syu

macOS Homebrew brew install package; brew upgrade

Windows winget winget install package; winget upgrade --all

Chapter 6: Package Management and Software

6.2 Working with apt

$ sudo apt update $ sudo apt upgrade $ apt search editor $ apt show nano $ sudo apt install tree $ sudo apt remove tree $ sudo apt autoremove $ apt list --installed

It is important to understand the difference between apt update, which refreshes the list of available packages and versions, and apt upgrade, which installs newer versions of packages you already have. Running update first ensures you see current information. The command apt autoremove deletes dependencies that are no longer needed.

Working with dnf, Homebrew, and winget

$ sudo dnf search nginx $ sudo dnf install nginx $ brew install wget $ brew update $ brew list $ winget search vscode $ winget install Microsoft.VisualStudioCode

The ideas carry across tools: search for a package, install it, upgrade regularly, and remove what you no longer need. Language ecosystems have their own package managers as well, such as pip for Python and npm for JavaScript; these install libraries for developers, usually into a project or user-specific location.

Good Practices

• Install software from official repositories whenever possible.

• Read the name of a package carefully; look-alike names are a known attack technique.

• Keep the system updated to receive security fixes.

• Review what a command will install before confirming, especially when it lists many dependencies.

• Avoid adding unknown third-party repositories without understanding who maintains them.

Lesson Summary

Package managers automate the installation, updating, and removal of software and its dependencies. Although command names differ among apt, dnf, Homebrew, and winget, they share a repository-based model that is safer and more maintainable than manual installation.

Chapter 6: Package Management and Software

6.3 Shell Scripting and Automation

From Commands to Scripts

A shell script is a text file containing commands that the shell executes in order. Scripts convert tasks you perform often into a single, reliable command. They are used for backups, deployments, system checks, data processing, and many other jobs. A script is simply the same commands you would type, plus logic that lets them make decisions and repeat work.

Create a file named hello.sh with the following content.

#!/bin/bash # A first script echo "Hello, $USER! Today is $(date +%A)."

The first line, called the shebang, tells the system which interpreter should run the file. Make the script executable and run it.

$ chmod +x hello.sh $ ./hello.sh

The prefix ./ tells the shell to run the file in the current directory, since the current directory is normally not in the PATH. You can also run a script with bash hello.sh without changing its permissions.

Variables and Input

Variables are assigned without spaces around the equals sign and read with a dollar sign. The read command accepts input from the user, and special variables give access to the arguments passed to a script.

#!/bin/bash name="Student" read -p "Enter your name: " name echo "Welcome, $name" echo "Script name: $0" echo "First argument: $1" echo "Number of arguments: $#" echo "All arguments: $@"

Variable Meaning

$0 The name of the script

$1, $2, ... The first, second, and later arguments

$# The number of arguments

$@ All arguments, each kept as a separate word when quoted

$? Exit status of the most recent command

Chapter 6: Package Management and Software

6.4 Variable

Meaning

$$ The process identifier of the current shell

Conditionals

The if statement runs commands depending on the exit status of a test. The [[ ... ]] construct in Bash and the older [ ... ] evaluate conditions.

#!/bin/bash file="$1" if [[ -f "$file" ]]; then echo "$file is a regular file" elif [[ -d "$file" ]]; then echo "$file is a directory" else echo "$file does not exist" fi

File test True if Number test True if

-e path The path exists -eq Numbers are equal

-f path It is a regular file -ne Not equal

-d path It is a directory -lt Less than

-r path It is readable -gt Greater than

-x path It is executable -le Less than or equal

-s path It exists and is not empty -ge Greater than or equal

String comparisons use == and != inside double brackets, and -z and -n test for empty and non-empty strings. Spaces inside the brackets are required. The case statement selects among several patterns and is neat for menus and option handling.

Loops

#!/bin/bash for f in *.txt; do echo "Processing $f" wc -l "$f" done

count=1 while [[ $count -le 5 ]]; do echo "Count: $count" count=$((count + 1)) done

for i in {1..3}; do echo "Round $i"; done

Chapter 6: Package Management and Software

6.5 The for loop repeats for each item in a list, such as the files matched by a wildcard. The while loop

repeats as long as its condition is true. Arithmetic is performed with $(( ... )). To read a file line by line, use while read -r line; do ... done < file.

Functions

A function groups commands under a name so they can be reused.

#!/bin/bash greet() { local who="$1" echo "Hello, $who!" } greet "Ada" greet "Linus"

The local keyword limits a variable to the function. A function returns an exit status with return; to deliver text, have it print the result and capture it with command substitution.

Exit Codes and Error Handling

Scripts should detect and report failure. Use exit with a number to end a script and communicate its outcome, with zero for success. Check commands whose failure matters.

#!/bin/bash set -euo pipefail if ! cp important.txt /backup/; then echo "Copy failed" >&2 exit 1 fi

The line set -euo pipefail is a widely used safety setting in Bash: -e exits when a command fails, -u treats use of an undefined variable as an error, and -o pipefail makes pipelines fail when any stage fails. Sending messages to standard error with >&2 keeps them separate from normal output. The trap command can run cleanup code when a script exits or is interrupted.

A Complete Example: A Backup Script

The following script checks its input, creates a timestamped archive, and reports the outcome. It uses nearly every concept from this chapter.

#!/bin/bash set -u src="$1" dest="$HOME/backups" stamp=$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S) archive="$dest/backup-$stamp.tar.gz"

if [[ ! -d "$src" ]]; then echo "Error: $src is not a directory" >&2

Chapter 6: Package Management and Software

6.6 exit 1

fi

mkdir -p "$dest" if tar -czf "$archive" "$src"; then echo "Backup created: $archive" else rm -f "$archive" echo "Backup failed" >&2 exit 2 fi

The decision flow of the backup script.

Scheduling with cron

The cron service runs commands on a schedule. Each user has a table of jobs called a crontab, edited with crontab -e and listed with crontab -l. A job line has five time fields followed by the command.

The five time fields of a crontab entry.

Chapter 6: Package Management and Software

6.7 $ crontab -e

30 2 * * 1 /home/student/backup.sh /home/student/Documents */15 * * * * /home/student/check-disk.sh 0 0 1 * * /usr/bin/apt-get update

An asterisk means every value, and */15 means every fifteenth. Jobs run in a minimal environment, so use full paths to programs and scripts, and redirect output to a log file, such as >> /home/student/cron.log 2>&1, so that you can diagnose problems. Systemd also supports scheduled tasks through timers, and the at command schedules a job to run once.

Script Quality and Debugging

Write scripts that others can read. Use meaningful names, add comments to explain why rather than what, quote variable expansions, and keep functions small. To debug, run a script with bash -x script.sh to display each command as it executes, or add set -x temporarily. The ShellCheck program analyzes scripts and warns about common mistakes; it is available as a website and a command-line tool. Always test destructive scripts on sample data before using them on real files.

Portability

A script that begins with #!/bin/sh should use only POSIX features. Features such as [[ ]], arrays, and brace ranges are Bash extensions, so use #!/bin/bash when you rely on them.

Lesson Summary

Shell scripting extends the command line with variables, decisions, loops, and functions. Good scripts check their inputs, handle errors, quote carefully, and report clearly. With cron, scripts can run automatically, turning one-time knowledge into reliable automation.

The Windows Command Line

Two Shells on Windows

Windows includes two main command-line environments. The Command Prompt (cmd.exe) is the long-standing shell inherited from MS-DOS and early Windows NT. PowerShell is a more modern shell and scripting language built on the .NET platform. Windows Terminal is a modern application that can host either one, as well as Linux distributions installed through the Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL), which allows a real Linux environment to run on Windows.

Chapter 7: Command Prompt Basics

7.1 Command Prompt Basics

Task Command Prompt Linux equivalent

Show current folder cd pwd

Change folder cd folder cd folder

List files dir ls

Clear the screen cls clear

Copy a file copy a b cp a b

Move or rename move a b or ren a b mv a b

Delete a file del file rm file

Make a directory mkdir name mkdir name

Show file contents type file cat file

Find text findstr "text" file grep "text" file

Network settings ipconfig ip addr

List processes tasklist ps

End a process taskkill /PID 1234 kill 1234

Help help or command /? man command

Windows paths use backslashes and drive letters, such as C:\Users\Student\Documents. Command options usually begin with a slash. Environment variables are referenced with percent signs, as in %USERPROFILE%. The pipe and redirection operators work in a way similar to Unix shells.

PowerShell Fundamentals

PowerShell commands, called cmdlets, follow a Verb-Noun naming pattern, which makes them easy to guess and discover: Get-Process, Stop-Process, Get-ChildItem, Copy-Item, and so on. Many common Unix names, such as ls, cp, and cat, exist as aliases that point to cmdlets. The key difference from traditional shells is that cmdlets pass objects, not just text, through pipelines. An object has named properties, so you can filter and select without parsing text columns.

PS C:\> Get-ChildItem PS C:\> Get-Process | Sort-Object CPU -Descending | Select-Object -First 5 PS C:\> Get-Service | Where-Object { $_.Status -eq "Running" } PS C:\> Get-Content log.txt | Select-String "error" PS C:\> Get-Help Get-Process -Examples PS C:\> Get-Command *service*

In these examples, Sort-Object orders objects by a property, Select-Object chooses properties or a number of items, Where-Object filters, and $_ represents the current object in the pipeline. The commands Get-Help and Get-Command help you discover cmdlets, and Get-Member shows the properties and methods of an object.

Chapter 7: Command Prompt Basics

7.2 Task

PowerShell cmdlet Common alias

List files Get-ChildItem ls, dir

Change folder Set-Location cd

Copy Copy-Item cp, copy

Move Move-Item mv, move

Delete Remove-Item rm, del

Show contents Get-Content cat, type

Display text Write-Output echo

List processes Get-Process ps

End a process Stop-Process kill

Scripting in PowerShell

PowerShell scripts are saved with the extension .ps1. Variables begin with a dollar sign, and the language includes if statements, loops, functions, and error handling with try and catch.

$files = Get-ChildItem -Path . -Filter *.txt foreach ($f in $files) { Write-Output "$($f.Name) has $($f.Length) bytes" }

Windows restricts script execution through an execution policy; check it with Get-ExecutionPolicy. Scripts from untrusted sources should be reviewed before they are run. PowerShell is also available on Linux and macOS, enabling shared automation across platforms.

Lesson Summary

Windows offers the Command Prompt for simple tasks and PowerShell for powerful, object-based administration. Many concepts transfer directly from Unix-like systems: navigation, redirection, pipelines, processes, and scripts. Learning the equivalent commands makes it easier to work on any system.

Chapter 7: Command Prompt Basics

7.3 Customization, Productivity, and Safe

Practice

Aliases

An alias is a short name for a longer command. Define aliases for tasks you perform often, and place them in your startup file to make them permanent.

$ alias ll='ls -alh' $ alias gs='git status' $ alias ..='cd ..' $ alias $ unalias ll

An alias is expanded as text, so it suits simple shortcuts. For anything involving arguments or logic, define a function instead.

Customizing the Prompt and Environment

In Bash, the prompt is controlled by the variable PS1. Special sequences stand for the user name, host name, and directory. For example, export PS1='\u@\h:\w\$ ' produces a prompt such as student@laptop:~/projects$. Keep prompts short and legible so that long directory names do not consume your line. Store customizations, along with aliases and environment variables, in your startup file and in a collection of configuration files known as dotfiles. Many people keep their dotfiles in a version-controlled repository so that a new computer can be set up in minutes.

Terminal Multiplexers

Programs such as tmux and screen let you run several terminal sessions inside one window and, critically, keep them alive when you disconnect. You can start a long task on a remote server, detach, close your laptop, and reattach later.

$ tmux new -s work $ tmux ls $ tmux attach -t work

Inside tmux, commands begin with a prefix key, by default Ctrl+B, followed by another key; for example, the prefix followed by d detaches the session.

Version Control from the Command Line

Git, the most widely used version control system, is primarily a command-line tool. A few commands cover daily use.

Chapter 7: Command Prompt Basics

7.4 $ git init

$ git status $ git add notes.txt $ git commit -m "Add notes" $ git log --oneline $ git diff

Version control records the history of your files, allows you to revert mistakes, and supports collaboration. Placing your scripts and configuration files under version control is one of the best habits you can build.

Working Efficiently

• Use Tab completion and history search constantly.

• Learn a few options of each command deeply rather than every option shallowly.

• Prefer small, composable steps and verify each stage.

• Keep a personal notes file of useful commands and one-liners.

• Read error messages carefully; they usually state the cause.

• Use the manual pages first, then search official documentation.

Safety and Professional Habits

The power of the command line comes with responsibility, because commands act immediately and often irreversibly. Adopt these habits.

• Look before you act. Run ls with a pattern before using the same pattern with rm. Use echo to preview a command that contains wildcards or variables.

• Use interactive and dry-run options. Options such as -i for confirmation and -n or --dry-run for simulation exist for a reason.

• Keep backups. Backups should be tested and stored in a separate location from the originals.

• Use least privilege. Work as a normal user and use sudo only when necessary.

• Do not run commands blindly. Understand each part of a command copied from a website or forum, especially anything that uses sudo, rm, dd, chmod -R, or downloads and runs scripts.

• Protect secrets. Do not place passwords or tokens in command arguments, scripts, or history. Use environment variables, secret managers, or key files with strict permissions.

• Quote variables. An unquoted, empty variable in a command such as rm -rf $DIR/ can have devastating consequences.

• Document and test. Comment your scripts and test them on sample data.

Key Idea

A careful professional is not someone who never makes mistakes. It is someone who builds habits, such as previews, backups, and least privilege, that make mistakes small and recoverable.

Chapter 7: Command Prompt Basics

7.5 Lesson Summary

Customization through aliases, prompts, dotfiles, multiplexers, and version control makes the command line comfortable and productive. Safe practices keep your work reliable. With the foundations from this book, you can continue exploring specialized tools in development, administration, data science, networking, and security.
